content_groups.group_title: Urgency Urinary Incontinence and Overactive Bladder

items.text: “A 55-year-old woman presents with urinary urgency and occasional leakage before reaching the toilet. Take a focused history and discuss management.”
“A woman complains of passing urine frequently during the day and waking several times at night. Assess her symptoms.”
“Counsel a patient newly diagnosed with overactive bladder.”
“Discuss the pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatment of urgency urinary incontinence.”

blocks.text: Main OSCE objective: Recognise urgency urinary incontinence, distinguish it from stress and other types of incontinence, identify reversible causes and red flags, and develop an individualised treatment plan.

Overactive bladder (OAB) is a symptom syndrome characterised by urinary urgency, usually accompanied by increased daytime frequency and nocturia, with or without urgency urinary incontinence, when urinary tract infection or another obvious cause has not been identified.
Urgency urinary incontinence (UUI) is involuntary urine leakage associated with, or immediately preceded by, a sudden compelling desire to pass urine that is difficult to defer.

items.text: OAB without incontinence: urgency, frequency and possibly nocturia, but no leakage.
OAB with urgency urinary incontinence: urgency accompanied by leakage before reaching the toilet.
Mixed urinary incontinence: both stress-related and urgency-related leakage.

blocks.text: During normal bladder filling, the detrusor muscle remains relaxed while the bladder stores urine. When appropriate, the nervous system coordinates detrusor contraction and urethral relaxation to allow voiding.

In OAB, the patient experiences urgency and other storage symptoms. Detrusor overactivity may be demonstrated during urodynamic testing in some patients, but it is not necessary to demonstrate detrusor overactivity to diagnose OAB clinically.

items.text: Diabetes mellitus and excessive urine production.
Bladder outlet or pelvic floor problems in selected patients.
Wash your hands and introduce yourself.
Explain that you will ask about urinary urgency, frequency, leakage and its effect on daily life.
Ensure privacy and offer a chaperone if an intimate examination is indicated.
Explain that you may recommend a urine test and, depending on the findings, a physical examination.

blocks.text: Example:

“Hello, I understand that you have been experiencing a frequent or sudden need to pass urine. I would like to ask you some questions to understand when it happens, whether you experience leakage, and how it affects your daily activities. I will then explain the possible causes and treatment options. Is that alright?”

items.text: “Can you describe the urinary problem you have been experiencing?”
“Has it become more frequent or severe?”

blocks.text: Establish duration, progression, frequency and severity.
Urgency is the defining symptom of OAB.

items.text: Do you experience a sudden, compelling need to pass urine?
Is it difficult to postpone urination once the urge begins?
Do you ever leak before reaching the toilet?
Does running water or arriving home trigger the urge?
Do you need to know where every toilet is when travelling?
Do you have to rush to the toilet immediately after feeling the urge?

blocks.text: Typical finding: the patient describes a sudden urge that is difficult to defer, sometimes followed by involuntary leakage.

items.text: How many times do you pass urine during the day?
How often do you wake at night to urinate?
Have you noticed a change from your usual pattern?
Do you pass large volumes or only small amounts each time?
Do you void frequently even when you have not consumed much fluid?

blocks.text: Frequent urination in small amounts may support a storage problem. Frequent passage of large volumes suggests polyuria and warrants assessment for causes such as diabetes or excessive fluid intake.

items.text: Is the leakage preceded by a sudden urge?
Does urine leak before you reach the toilet?
Does leakage occur with coughing, sneezing, laughing or exercise?
Do you use pads or change clothes?
Is there continuous leakage even when you do not feel an urge?

blocks.text: This helps distinguish urgency, stress, mixed, overflow and possible fistula-related leakage.

items.text: Recurrent leakage or dribbling after voiding.

blocks.text: Dysuria and acute worsening may suggest infection. Hesitancy, a weak stream or incomplete emptying may indicate retention or voiding dysfunction.

content_groups.group_title: F. Fluid intake and dietary triggers

items.text: Tea, coffee, energy drinks and cola.
Excessive thirst or large urine volumes.

blocks.text: Do not automatically advise severe fluid restriction. The aim is appropriate hydration and reduction of individual bladder irritants where they appear to worsen symptoms.

content_groups.group_title: G. Medical, neurological and medication history

items.text: Stroke, multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease or spinal disease.
Current medicines, particularly diuretics and drugs that may impair bladder emptying.
Sexual symptoms and impact on intimacy, if relevant.

content_groups.group_title: I. Impact on quality of life

blocks.title: Ask whether the symptoms interfere with:

items.text: Difficulty passing urine or suspected retention.
New neurological symptoms, including leg weakness or saddle sensory loss.
Recurrent symptoms that are atypical or unexplained.

blocks.text: New neurological deficits with acute urinary retention, saddle sensory loss or leg weakness require urgent assessment for possible neurological compression.

Examination is guided by the history. Not every woman with uncomplicated OAB requires a comprehensive pelvic examination, but examination is appropriate when symptoms are complex, there are red flags, prolapse is suspected or another diagnosis needs exclusion.

items.text: Mobility and ability to reach the toilet.
Peripheral oedema, particularly if nocturia is prominent.
Assess for a palpable, distended bladder.

blocks.text: A distended bladder may suggest retention rather than uncomplicated OAB.

blocks.title: With consent and a chaperone where appropriate, assess:

items.text: Signs of genitourinary syndrome of menopause.
Pelvic masses or tenderness when indicated.
Evidence of urine leakage if the history suggests stress or mixed incontinence.

blocks.text: If indicated, assess lower-limb power, sensation, reflexes and relevant sacral neurological function. Abnormal findings should prompt further evaluation.

rows: Urinary tract infection
Dysuria, suprapubic pain, acute worsening of urgency or frequency
Stress urinary incontinence
Leakage triggered by coughing, sneezing or physical exertion
Mixed urinary incontinence
Both urgency-related and stress-related leakage
Diabetes mellitus
Polyuria, polydipsia and often large urine volumes
Nocturnal polyuria
Disproportionately high urine production at night
Overflow incontinence
Retention, weak stream, incomplete emptying and dribbling
Pelvic organ prolapse
Vaginal bulge or pressure, sometimes with voiding dysfunction
Bladder pain syndrome
Bladder-associated pain or pressure, often related to filling, with urinary frequency
Neurological bladder dysfunction
Relevant neurological history or abnormal neurological examination
Vesicovaginal fistula
Persistent or continuous watery vaginal leakage, often after pelvic surgery or obstructed labour

blocks.text: Exam pearl: Frequency alone does not establish OAB. Urgency is the central symptom, and infection, polyuria and other identifiable causes should be considered.

rows: Urinalysis
Initial assessment for blood, glucose and evidence of infection
Urine culture
When symptoms or urinalysis suggest infection
Bladder diary, usually for at least 3 days
Documents fluid intake, voiding times, volumes, urgency, leakage and nocturia
Blood glucose or HbA1c
If diabetes or polyuria is suspected
Post-void residual measurement
If voiding difficulty, retention, recurrent infection or relevant neurological disease is suspected
Renal function tests
When renal disease or another relevant medical indication is present
Urodynamic studies
Selected complex or uncertain cases; not routine for uncomplicated OAB
Cystoscopy or imaging
Only when specific features or suspected pathology warrant them

content_groups.group_title: How to interpret a bladder diary

items.text: Time and amount of each drink.
Time and volume of each urination.

blocks.text: This can help distinguish frequent small-volume voiding from excessive urine production and identify modifiable triggers.
Management is usually stepwise and tailored to the patient's symptoms, preferences, comorbidities and treatment response.

content_groups.group_title: A. First-line: behavioural and lifestyle measures

blocks.text: 1. Bladder training
This is a key first-line intervention, especially when urgency and urgency incontinence are present.
The patient follows a planned voiding schedule and gradually extends the interval between voids, while learning strategies to suppress urgency.
2. Fluid and dietary modification
Maintain adequate hydration, avoid excessive fluid intake, and reduce caffeine if it worsens symptoms. Adjust evening intake when nocturia is troublesome, while avoiding dehydration.
3. Treat contributing factors
Address constipation, manage diabetes and other relevant medical conditions, review medications where appropriate, and encourage weight management if indicated.

items.text: Explain that the bladder can become accustomed to frequent voiding.
Ask the patient to record her usual voiding intervals in a diary.
Encourage her to delay voiding gradually rather than rushing immediately at every mild sensation.
Teach urgency suppression: stop moving, remain still or sit if needed, breathe slowly, relax, and perform a few quick pelvic floor contractions if able.
Once the urge settles, walk calmly to the toilet.
Review progress and adapt the plan.

blocks.text: Do not ask the patient to endure severe pain or force prolonged delays. The plan should be practical and tailored to her symptoms.

Pelvic floor muscle training may be helpful, particularly for women with urgency urinary incontinence or coexisting stress incontinence. Teach correct contraction and consider supervised physiotherapy.
For mixed urinary incontinence, treatment should address both components rather than treating urgency alone.
Medication may be offered if behavioural treatment is insufficient, symptoms remain troublesome, or the patient prefers medication after discussion of options.
Two important groups are used:
**1. Antimuscarinic medicines**
Mechanism: Reduce muscarinic receptor-mediated detrusor activity and may improve urgency, frequency and urgency leakage.

items.text: Possible cognitive adverse effects, particularly with medicines that have greater central nervous system penetration and in susceptible older adults.

blocks.text: Assess the patient's risk of urinary retention, constipation, cognitive impairment and other contraindications before prescribing.
**2. Beta-3 adrenergic agonists**
Examples include mirabegron and, where available and approved, vibegron.
Mechanism: Promote bladder storage by relaxing the detrusor during the filling phase.
Potential advantages include fewer dry-mouth and constipation effects than many antimuscarinics.

items.text: Mirabegron can increase blood pressure and should be used cautiously or avoided in severe uncontrolled hypertension according to product guidance.
Assess for urinary retention risk and relevant drug interactions.
Availability and prescribing recommendations vary by setting.

blocks.text: Clinical principle: Select the medicine according to patient-specific risks, contraindications, availability, cost and local guidelines. Review effectiveness and adverse effects after initiation.

For a postmenopausal patient with vaginal dryness, irritation or other genitourinary symptoms, vaginal oestrogen may be considered when appropriate. It treats associated menopausal tissue symptoms but is not a substitute for a complete OAB assessment.

content_groups.group_title: F. Specialist referral and advanced treatments

blocks.text: Refer when symptoms are severe, diagnosis is uncertain, red flags are present, initial treatment fails or the patient needs advanced options.

blocks.title: Options available in specialist care may include:

blocks.text: These require counselling about benefits, risks, follow-up and practical requirements. For example, bladder botulinum toxin may cause urinary retention and urinary tract infection, and some patients may need intermittent self-catheterisation.
A possible OSCE counselling response:

“Your symptoms suggest that your bladder is giving you a sudden and difficult-to-control urge to pass urine. This is often called overactive bladder, although we need to check for infection and other possible causes before confirming the diagnosis.

The good news is that several treatments can improve symptoms. We can begin with a bladder diary, bladder training, appropriate fluid habits and reducing caffeine if it is a trigger. If symptoms remain troublesome, medicines are available. These can help, although they may cause side effects, so we would choose one that is suitable for you and review how you respond.

If the symptoms do not improve, or if there are concerning features, we may arrange further investigations or refer you to a specialist. You should seek medical assessment if you develop blood in your urine, significant pain, difficulty passing urine or new neurological symptoms.”
Check understanding and invite questions. Reassure the patient that symptoms are common and treatment can be individualised.

subsections.subsection_title: 11. How to present findings in an OSCE

content_groups.group_title: Example A: Uncomplicated OAB with urgency incontinence

blocks.text: “This patient reports sudden compelling urinary urgency, increased daytime frequency and episodes of leakage before reaching the toilet. She does not report leakage with coughing or exertion. There are no reported red flags. The history is suggestive of urgency urinary incontinence, within the overactive bladder syndrome. I would perform urinalysis, review fluid intake and medications, obtain a bladder diary and offer bladder training with follow-up.”

content_groups.group_title: Example B: OAB symptoms with possible infection

blocks.text: “The patient has urgency and frequency associated with dysuria and suprapubic discomfort. These findings raise suspicion of urinary tract infection rather than uncomplicated OAB alone. I would perform urinalysis and obtain a urine culture when indicated, then manage the suspected infection according to clinical assessment and local guidance before reassessing persistent symptoms.”

content_groups.group_title: Example C: OAB symptoms with polyuria

blocks.text: “The patient reports frequency and nocturia but passes large volumes of urine and describes excessive thirst. This raises concern for polyuria, including possible diabetes mellitus, rather than isolated OAB. I would assess fluid intake, check blood glucose and investigate other causes as indicated.”

content_groups.group_title: Example D: OAB symptoms with voiding difficulty

blocks.text: “The patient has urgency and frequency but also reports a weak stream and incomplete bladder emptying. This raises concern for voiding dysfunction or urinary retention. I would measure the post-void residual volume and arrange further assessment before initiating treatment that could worsen retention.”
Q1. What is the defining symptom of OAB?
Urinary urgency: a sudden compelling desire to pass urine that is difficult to defer.
Q2. Must urgency urinary incontinence be present for OAB?
No. OAB can occur without leakage. Urgency incontinence is present when involuntary leakage accompanies or immediately follows urgency.
Q3. Is detrusor overactivity required to diagnose OAB?
No. OAB is a clinical symptom syndrome. Detrusor overactivity is a urodynamic finding and is not required for the clinical diagnosis.
Q4. What is the initial investigation?
Urinalysis is part of the initial assessment. A bladder diary is also very useful for characterising symptoms and fluid intake.
Q5. What is the first-line treatment?
Bladder training and appropriate behavioural and lifestyle measures, with pelvic floor muscle training where indicated.
Q6. What is the difference between OAB and stress urinary incontinence?
OAB is characterised by urgency, often with frequency and nocturia, and may include urgency-related leakage. SUI causes leakage with coughing, sneezing or exertion.
Q7. Name two drug classes used for OAB.
Antimuscarinic medicines and beta-3 adrenergic agonists.
Q8. What are the main adverse effects of antimuscarinics?
Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, possible urinary retention and potential cognitive adverse effects in susceptible patients.
Q9. Why should blood pressure be considered before prescribing mirabegron?
Mirabegron can increase blood pressure and may be unsuitable in severe uncontrolled hypertension.
Q10. When is a post-void residual measurement useful?
When there is difficulty voiding, suspected retention, recurrent infection or relevant neurological disease.
Q11. What advanced treatment options are available for refractory OAB?
Intradetrusor botulinum toxin, sacral neuromodulation and tibial nerve stimulation, depending on specialist assessment, suitability and availability.
Q12. What is the role of cystoscopy and urodynamics?
Neither is routinely required for uncomplicated OAB. They may be appropriate when there is diagnostic uncertainty, suspected underlying pathology or a need for specialist assessment.

items.text: Diagnosing OAB based on frequency alone without asking about urgency.
Failing to distinguish urgency leakage from stress leakage.
Ignoring dysuria, haematuria or recurrent infections.
Failing to consider diabetes when the patient passes large volumes of urine.
Prescribing an antimuscarinic without considering constipation, cognitive effects or retention risk.
Prescribing mirabegron without considering blood pressure and contraindications.
Ordering urodynamics or cystoscopy routinely in uncomplicated cases.
Forgetting to assess the impact on sleep and quality of life.
R — Rule out infection and red flags.
G — Gauge frequency, nocturia and leakage.
E — Evaluate fluid intake, medicines and medical causes.
C — Commence bladder training and appropriate lifestyle measures.
Y — Your treatment plan should be individualised and reviewed.
